chapter_title: Deploying the dApp to IPFS/Decentralized Hosting

screens.title: Deploying the dApp to IPFS / Decentralized Hosting
screens.subtitle: Complete the decentralization stack by publishing your frontend as immutable IPFS content and pinning it for reliable availability.

narration.text: In this lesson we finish the decentralization story by moving the frontend off a centralized server and onto IPFS. You will learn why a peer‑to‑peer file system matters for censorship resistance and integrity, and how to convert your React app into static artifacts suitable for IPFS. I’ll show you the end‑to‑end workflow: build the app, upload the build folder using a pinning service such as Pinata, obtain the content identifier, and optionally update an ENS contenthash so users can visit your dApp with a human‑readable name. Along the way we’ll cover essential safety practices: store A P I keys in environment variables or CI secrets, pin content to prevent garbage collection, and plan for immutability — every update produces a new CID. By the end you’ll understand practical steps to make your dApp resilient and why pinning and name resolution matter. Think about one small change to your frontend — how would you publish that change and keep links working? That question frames our stepwise walkthrough.

keyIdea.title: Why host the frontend on IPFS?
keyIdea.text: Hosting the frontend on IPFS makes your dApp immutable, censorship‑resistant, and reachable by CID or ENS contenthash so the entire user experience is decentralized.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.8 › Deploy to IPFS

Deploy the dApp to IPFS

Follow a reproducible, secure process to publish your production build to IPFS and ensure it stays available and verifiable.

Interactive 16:9 Masterclass
Terminal demo style — build, pin, verify
In this lesson
Build

Compile your React app into static files using the project's build script so the result can be uploaded to IPFS.

Pin

Use a pinning service like Pinata to pin your build directory so the CID remains available on the network.

Resolve

Optionally point an ENS contenthash to the CID so users can reach your dApp with a .eth name.

Concept snapshot
IPFS CID
A cryptographic hash addressing your static build. Any change creates a new CID.
Access example
https://ipfs.io/ipfs/<YOUR_CID>/ or via a Pinata gateway to load your deployed dApp.
Key Takeaway

Decentralize both smart contracts and frontend files to achieve full censorship resistance and integrity for your dApp.

Coming up

We’ll start by preparing the React build, then show manual and scripted uploads to Pinata, and finish with safety notes and CI/CD considerations.

screens.title: Learning Objectives
screens.subtitle: Skills you'll be able to demonstrate after this chapter

narration.text: Over the next series of screens you will gain practical skills that make a dApp frontend production‑ready and decentralized. First, you will understand decentralized hosting and why IPFS provides immutability and censorship resistance. Second, you will be able to build a React/Vite frontend into a static artifact folder ready for upload. Third, you will learn how to create and protect Pinata A P I keys and use a script or the web UI to pin your build. Finally, you will learn the optional step of updating an ENS contenthash so users can access your dApp with a human readable name. Each objective pairs hands‑on steps with security checks so you can deploy safely in real projects. For example, when we generate an A P I key we will show how to store it in environment variables or CI secrets to avoid accidental exposure. By the end you will not only perform these steps but explain why each step preserves decentralization and what can go wrong.

keyIdea.title: Practical competence
keyIdea.text: You will be able to produce a build, pin it to IPFS, and keep deployment secrets safe while optionally linking a .eth name to your CID.

screens.title: Further objectives and practical checks
screens.subtitle: Tasks and checks you can perform to verify deployment success

narration.text: These additional objectives focus on verification and optional name resolution. You will learn how to verify your deployed build by visiting the IPFS gateway URL and checking that your dApp loads and interacts with the existing smart contracts. Next, you will practice updating an ENS contenthash so the. eth name resolves to your CID; this is optional but shows how to present a friendly address to users. We also emphasize the consequence of immutability: every update generates a new CID and requires updating any pinned links or ENS records. Finally, you will run through a CI checklist for automation: run tests, build the frontend, pin to IPFS programmatically, and rotate A P I keys securely. These objectives prepare you to deploy repeatedly and safely, and to explain to others why pinning and secret management are essential parts of dApp operations.

keyIdea.title: Verify and automate
keyIdea.text: Confirm the CID loads your app and set up pipelines that rebuild, pin, and update references while protecting secrets.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.8 › Verification & Automation
Checklist
  • Load test: Visit the gateway URL for the CID and confirm wallet connectivity and contract calls work.
  • ENS update: If using ENS, set the domain's contenthash to the new CID so users can reach the app via .eth.
  • Immutability check: Remember that any code change creates a new CID and requires updating pointers.
  • Pin persistence: Confirm Pinata shows the content as pinned and has not expired under your plan.
Try this

Open the gateway link and perform a state‑changing action through your dApp to verify end‑to‑end connectivity to the deployed contract.

Pitfall

Do not commit API keys. Use CI secrets and environment variables to avoid exposing credentials that can re-pin or remove your content.

Quick reference
Gateway example: https://ipfs.io/ipfs/<CID>/
ENS record: Update contenthash to point at your CID for friendly names.
CI flow: test → build → pin → update ENS (optional).
Why it matters

Verification confirms your dApp is not only reachable but functions with your deployed contracts, ensuring a complete decentralized stack.

screens.title: What is IPFS and why it matters for dApps
screens.subtitle: Peer‑to‑peer content addressing, immutability, and pinning explained

narration.text: IPFS is a peer‑to‑peer content network that addresses files by content rather than location. That means each build you upload to IPFS receives a cryptographic content identifier, or CID, derived from the file bytes. If any file changes, the CID changes too. For dApps this is useful because the frontend can be verified by its CID and served by any node that has the content. Pinning is the mechanism that keeps a particular node from discarding content; a service like Pinata pins your folder so at least one reliable node serves it. A concrete example: you build your React site and pin the dist directory; the network gives you a CID. Users can open the CID through a gateway and see the exact assets you published. A common misconception is that IPFS automatically keeps content forever — it does not. Without pinning, content may be garbage‑collected if no nodes hold it. Another misconception is that a CID is mutable; it is immutable. The practical takeaway is to pin critical releases and plan how to update pointers such as ENS contenthashes when you publish a new CID. How would you ensure the latest release remains reachable even after many updates?

keyIdea.title: Content addressing vs location
keyIdea.text: IPFS identifies content by a cryptographic hash (CID). Pinning keeps that content available; without pinning, availability is not guaranteed.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.8 › IPFS Fundamentals
Definition
IPFS: content addressing and immutability

IPFS assigns a CID to content. That CID is a verifiable fingerprint of the files you uploaded. If anything changes, the fingerprint changes too.

Analogy

Think of the CID as the SHA fingerprint of a release artifact. The fingerprint guarantees integrity, like a signed release tarball.

Common misconception

IPFS does not guarantee permanence by itself; pinning is required to keep content hosted on reliable nodes.

Key Takeaway

Use IPFS for integrity and censorship resistance, and use pinning services to maintain availability for production dApps.

Example
After running your build, upload and pin the dist folder. Pinning yields a CID you can share. A user who loads the CID gets exactly the files you uploaded; any later change will produce a different CID.
How to ensure availability
  • Pin the CID with a service like Pinata to guarantee at least one stable host.
  • Consider running your own IPFS node as a long‑term pinning strategy for critical releases.
  • Update any name records (such as ENS) whenever you publish a new CID.
Closing prompt: Which release would you pin first — a hotfix or a major redesign — and how would you update pointers to avoid downtime?

screens.title: Prepare your React dApp for IPFS
screens.subtitle: Build commands, output folders, and verifying the dist directory

narration.text: Before you upload anything to IPFS you must produce a production build that contains only static assets. In React projects the standard step is to run the project's build script — for example, run the build command that the project uses, commonly npm run build. Vite projects output a dist folder by default; other setups may use build. This folder contains optimized H T M L, JavaScript bundles, C S S, and static assets like images. Verify the folder by opening index. html locally or serving it with a simple static server to confirm client routing, environment configuration, and wallet connectors still work. A concrete example: run the build, inspect dist/index. html to ensure correct asset links, and test that the dApp can read contract addresses from a configuration file or environment placeholder that was baked into the build. A common mistake is deploying the dev build or forgetting to set the production RPC endpoints and contract addresses prior to building. The key takeaway is to treat the dist folder as the single source of truth for what you upload to IPFS, and to verify it in a local static server before pinning.

keyIdea.title: Build once, verify once
keyIdea.text: Produce a production build, confirm assets and contract endpoints are correct, and then upload the dist directory to IPFS.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.8 › Build & Verify
Terminal demo
$ cd my-solidity-dapp-frontend
$ npm run build
# Vite outputs: dist/
# Create: dist/index.html
# Create: dist/assets/*.js
# Create: dist/assets/*.css
After the build completes, inspect the dist folder. Confirm that index.html references the generated asset filenames and that any environment values (API endpoints, contract addresses) were baked in during build time.
Verification step

Serve the dist folder locally with a static server and walk through the UI to ensure wallet integration and contract calls succeed.

Common mistake

Deploying an unbuilt project or a development build will break asset references and routing when served statically from IPFS.

Checklist
  • Confirm build output directory name (dist or build) for your toolchain.
  • Verify asset paths in index.html and ensure routing works when served statically.
  • Ensure production RPC and contract addresses were set before building.
Key Takeaway

The build output is the single artifact you will pin to IPFS — validate it thoroughly before uploading.

screens.title: Scripted upload to IPFS using ipfs-http-client
screens.subtitle: A deploy script walkthrough using ipfs-http-client and Pinata headers

narration.text: Uploading programmatically makes deployments repeatable and automatable in CI. The chapter supplies a small deploy script that uses ipfs‑http‑client and Pinata credentials via HTTP headers for authentication. The script walks the dist directory, yields files to ipfs. addAll with options like pin and wrapWithDirectory, and captures the root CID for the wrapped directory. A concrete example is the deploy‑ipfs. js script: it creates an ipfs client pointed at ipfs. pinata. cloud with authorization set as Basic and then iterates the build folder to stream files into addAll. After the upload completes the script prints the root CID that becomes the permanent address of your release. A common pitfall is hardcoding A P I keys in the script — instead export them as environment variables or inject them as CI secrets. Another mistake is not wrapping files in a directory; without wrapWithDirectory you might get many individual CIDs rather than a single directory CID. The practical outcome is an automated step you can add to a CI pipeline that builds, pins, and returns a CID for subsequent steps like ENS updates.

keyIdea.title: Automate with care
keyIdea.text: Use a deployment script to upload and pin the build, but keep credentials in environment variables and use wrapWithDirectory to receive a single root CID.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.8 › Deploy Script
Code walkthrough
import { create } from 'ipfs-http-client'
import fs from 'fs'
import path from 'path'

const projectId = process.env.PINATA_KEY
const projectSecret = process.env.PINATA_SECRET
const auth = 'Basic ' + Buffer.from(projectId + ':' + projectSecret).toString('base64')

const ipfs = create({ host: 'ipfs.pinata.cloud', port: 5001, protocol: 'https', headers: { authorization: auth } })

async function deploy() {
  const buildPath = path.join(process.cwd(), 'dist')
  // generator yields file objects for ipfs.addAll
  const result = await ipfs.addAll(getFiles(buildPath), { pin: true, wrapWithDirectory: true })
  // iterate result to find the root CID and print it
}
Note: export your PINATA_KEY and PINATA_SECRET to the environment before running the script. In CI, store them as repository secrets and inject them into the job.
Gotcha

If you forget wrapWithDirectory you may get separate CIDs for each file rather than a single root CID for the site.

Pro tip

Pin incrementally for large sites and capture the root CID last, so uploads can resume and be verified stepwise.

Example output
Successfully deployed to IPFS!
Root CID: Qm...YourRootCID
Access: https://ipfs.io/ipfs/Qm...YourRootCID/
Security reminder

Never commit API keys. Use environment variables locally and secrets in your CI provider when automating deployments.

screens.title: Pinata, pinning, and access patterns
screens.subtitle: Choose a pinning option, verify availability, and understand immutability implications

narration.text: Pinning services like Pinata provide a reliable, managed way to keep your CID available without running your own IPFS node. You have two common options: the web interface for manual uploads and a programmatic A P I for CI automation. The web UI is great for quick tests: upload the dist folder, get a CID, and verify the app via a gateway. For production, use the A P I or ipfs‑http‑client in a deployment script so builds are reproducible. Pinning ensures at least one node will serve your content; without pinning, the network might prune your files. A practical example: upload via Pinata's folder uploader to get a CID, then add an ENS contenthash to map mydapp. eth to that CID for friendly access. A common misconception is thinking ENS points to mutable content. ENS stores a contenthash value; when your CID changes after an update you must write the new contenthash into ENS. Finally, plan for pin persistence: review your pinning service's retention terms and consider running your own node for guaranteed long‑term availability. The learner question is: which pin strategy fits your app's update cadence and availability needs?

keyIdea.title: Pick a pinning strategy
keyIdea.text: Manual pinning is fine for testing; API‑based pinning and self‑hosted nodes are better for production and high availability.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.8 › Pinata & Pinning
Comparison: Web UI vs Programmatic
Web UI

Fast for manual uploads and small releases. Good for initial testing and one‑off pins.

Programmatic/API

Automatable and repeatable for CI. Allows scripts to capture the CID and feed it into downstream steps like ENS updates.

Decision guide: use the web UI for quick tests and the API for CI/CD deployments to guarantee reproducibility and traceability.
Immutability & ENS

When you update files, IPFS returns a new CID. ENS contenthash is a pointer to a CID. To serve a new release under the same human‑readable name you must update the ENS record to the new CID. This is a manual or scripted step in your CI pipeline.

Common mistake

Assuming ENS will follow your updates automatically. ENS points to a specific CID; you must update it when you publish a new CID.

Key Takeaway

Choose a pinning approach that matches your release cadence and ensure ENS updates are part of your deployment pipeline if you want a stable user‑visible domain.

screens.title: Security and CI/CD considerations
screens.subtitle: Protect keys, automate builds, and plan for CID immutability in pipelines

narration.text: When you automate deployments, security and careful pipeline design matter. First, store Pinata A P I keys outside version control in environment variables or CI secret stores. In a GitHub Actions or GitLab CI job, inject these secrets at runtime so the deployment script can read them without exposing them to the repository. Second, structure your CI pipeline into discrete steps: run frontend and Solidity tests, build the frontend, run the deploy script to Pinata and capture the root CID, then optionally call an ENS update step to set the new contenthash. Third, add verification and rollback steps: after deployment, run an automated smoke test against the gateway URL to ensure the new CID serves the dApp and that wallet interactions function. Finally, accept immutability as a design constraint — plan to manage historical CIDs and provide redirects or versioned names if your app needs backward compatibility. A common misconception is that automating deployment removes the need for manual verification; it does not. Always include a verification stage and take care to rotate or revoke A P I keys if they are compromised. Think about how you would protect the deployment pipeline if someone gained access to your CI secrets.

keyIdea.title: Safe automation
keyIdea.text: CI pipelines should build, pin, verify, and optionally update ENS while secrets remain protected and verification prevents accidental breakage in production.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.8 › CI/CD & Security
CI/CD steps
  1. Run unit tests for contracts and frontend tests.
  2. Build the frontend (npm run build).
  3. Run deploy script to upload and pin; capture root CID as an output variable.
  4. Optionally update ENS contenthash using the CID.
  5. Run a smoke test against the gateway URL to verify functionality.
Secrets

Use CI secret stores for API keys and rotate them periodically. Never print secrets into logs.

Verification

Include an automated smoke test step that loads the deployed CID and performs a minimal contract interaction.

Safety notes
  • Never hardcode keys in the repository; use environment variables or CI secrets.
  • Be aware that immutability requires pointer updates when you release new CIDs.
  • Pin critical releases and review pin retention policies of your pinning provider.
Key Takeaway

Automate the build and pin steps, protect secrets, and always verify the deployed CID to keep your dApp reliable and secure.

screens.title: Accessing your deployed dApp via IPFS gateways
screens.subtitle: How to verify a CID and confirm the dApp functions in the browser

narration.text: After you upload static assets to IPFS and receive a root CID, the next step is to verify that your dApp actually loads and that wallet interactions still work. Accessing an IPFS-hosted site is as simple as opening a gateway URL with the CID, for example: open the gateway URL that ends with the root CID and a trailing slash. When you load the site, check three practical things: the static H T M L/C S S/JS assets must load without 404 errors, your Web3 provider should prompt wallet connection, and contract calls should behave the same as when served from a centralized host. One concrete example: if your root CID is QmExampleCid, open the URL that looks like https://ipfs. io/ipfs/QmExampleCid/. If the site fails to connect to your contract, inspect the browser console for network errors and verify the built files reference absolute or relative endpoints correctly. A common misconception is that IPFS magically solves runtime connectivity; IPFS only hosts static files — your frontend still needs to reach RPC endpoints, wallets, and contract addresses. That means ENS or environment-driven addresses must still be configured. If a single asset fails to load, the CID may have been built from a different directory or there may be an incorrect base path in your build. As a final verification step, test the dApp in an incognito window and from another machine to confirm pinning and gateway propagation. How would you confirm that your deployed CID serves the same production bundle you built locally?

keyIdea.title: Verify the CID and runtime connections
keyIdea.text: Open the gateway URL for your root CID, confirm asset loads and wallet/contract interactions, and check console/network errors to diagnose missing files or base-path issues.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.8 › Access & Verification
Process
Open the gateway URL
Use an IPFS gateway URL to load your root CID and verify that the static bundle serves correctly and that wallet connections prompt as expected.
Example gateway URLs
https://ipfs.io/ipfs/QmYourRootCid/
https://gateway.pinata.cloud/ipfs/QmYourRootCid/

Open one of these in your browser and verify the app loads.
Checklist
  • All assets (index.html, CSS, JS) return 200 via the gateway.
  • Wallet connection prompts and RPC endpoints are reachable from the site.
  • No 404s in the network tab and no mixed-content errors.
Key Takeaway

A successful gateway load plus wallet prompts means the frontend is reachable; runtime failures usually point to configuration, not IPFS itself.

Common Mistake

Using absolute dev-server paths in the build can break production assets when served from IPFS. Ensure the build uses correct base paths.

Example Verification Walkthrough
A quick manual flow to confirm behavior and isolate problems.
  1. Open the gateway URL for the CID and watch the network tab for failed requests.
  2. Attempt to connect your wallet; confirm the provider window appears.
  3. Trigger a simple read-only contract call and observe the response or console errors.
  4. If a request fails, compare the file paths in the built bundle to the IPFS directory listing returned by your pinning service.
Scenario
Imagine the app loads but wallet calls fail: often the frontend still points to a local RPC URL. Update environment variables in the build and redeploy to get a new CID, then retest.

screens.title: Mapping an ENS name to your IPFS CID
screens.subtitle: How to point a human-readable .eth name to your dApp's CID

narration.text: Linking a human-readable ENS name to your IPFS-hosted dApp gives users a familiar address and a smoother experience. ENS stores a contenthash record that can contain an IPFS CID. Conceptually, you set the contenthash for your ENS domain to the CID produced when you uploaded your dist folder. The chapter suggests doing this through the ENS registrar interface, which is the simplest and most common approach: you sign in with the wallet that controls the ENS name, open the domain's records, and set the contenthash field to the new CID. A concrete example: after uploading and obtaining the CID, navigate to your ENS management UI, find the contenthash entry, paste the CID, and confirm the transaction from your connected wallet. Remember this is optional; ENS adds a human-friendly layer but is not required for IPFS access. A frequent misconception is that ENS changes the content on IPFS — it does not. It only points the name to a given CID. Because IPFS is immutable, any change to your site produces a new CID and therefore requires updating the ENS contenthash to keep the name pointing at the latest version. Finally, consider gas and ownership: changing a contenthash is an on-chain transaction and requires the ENS name owner to sign it, so keep the ENS private keys and signing process secure. How will you manage updating ENS when you publish routine frontend fixes?

keyIdea.title: ENS points names to CIDs
keyIdea.text: Set the ENS contenthash to your IPFS CID using the ENS management interface; updates require a signed transaction and produce a new contenthash when your site changes.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.8 › ENS Integration
Set the contenthash
Use the ENS manager to paste your IPFS CID into the domain's contenthash record and confirm the update.
Steps:
  1. Connect the wallet that owns the ENS name.
  2. Open the domain's records and choose contenthash.
  3. Paste the CID you received from your pinning service and save the change.
  4. Confirm the on-chain transaction and wait for block confirmation.
Practical note

Setting contenthash requires signing a transaction and paying gas. Keep your ENS keys secure and consider automating updates through a CI/CD step that calls a verified contract method or script.

Why it matters

ENS makes your dApp discoverable with a human-readable name while remaining decentralized because the name points to an immutable CID.

Quick UI mock of the ENS contenthash field
Domain
mydapp.eth
Contenthash (paste CID)
QmYourRootCid
Pressing 'Save' triggers an ENS transaction to update the record.
Misconception

ENS does not host your files. It is a pointer. If no node pins the CID, the content may be unavailable even if the ENS record points to it.

screens.title: Managing updates: new CIDs, versioning, and pointers
screens.subtitle: Strategies to handle immutable CIDs when you change your frontend

narration.text: One defining property of IPFS is immutability: any change to your built files produces a new cryptographic content identifier, so updating your dApp means you will get a new CID. That behavior provides integrity but requires a strategy for versioning and pointer updates. A typical workflow is: build the new frontend, upload to IPFS and pin it, obtain the new CID, then update any human-readable pointer such as an ENS contenthash or a static redirect that you control. For example, if you published version 1 with CID A and later publish version 2 with CID B, you can update the ENS record to point to CID B so users that open your ENS name land on the new bundle. Another option is to maintain a changelog page and advertise versioned CIDs for reproducibility. A common mistake is assuming old CIDs will automatically update — they won’t. Pinning services may retain older versions, so coordinate pin lifecycles if you expect to roll back. Also plan how you will communicate the update: because CIDs are immutable, bookmarks and external links that contain a CID must be updated wherever they appear. Finally, think about cache and gateway propagation: some public gateways and caches may still serve older content briefly. The learner question to reflect on is: which pointer strategy fits your release cadence — frequent updates need automation, while infrequent releases may be fine with manual ENS edits?

keyIdea.title: New content means new CID
keyIdea.text: Treat every deploy as a new immutable artifact. Use ENS, published changelogs, or automation to switch pointers and communicate updates to users.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.8 › Immutability & Versioning
Release timeline
  1. Build the frontend to produce a production dist folder.
  2. Upload & pin the dist directory to IPFS; receive root CID.
  3. Update pointers such as ENS contenthash to the new CID.
  4. Verify via gateway and user tests, then remove or keep previous pins as needed.
Versioning strategies
1) ENS pointer updates for a single canonical name — best when you control the name and prefer a single landing page.
2) Release-specific CIDs with a public changelog for reproducibility and archival.
3) Automation in CI to update ENS and pin the new CID immediately after tests pass — useful for frequent releases.
Rollback
Keep previous CIDs pinned if you may need to revert. Repoint ENS to the prior CID to roll back quickly.
Cache timing
Allow for gateway caching; a small propagation delay can occur after updating pointers. Verify from multiple gateways.
Audit trail
Publish release notes with CID values so users can verify the exact deployed bundle used in each release.

screens.title: Review: deploy-ipfs.js and environment security
screens.subtitle: How the example script uploads a directory and why secrets must be protected

narration.text: The example deployment script in the chapter uses the ipfs-http-client to add all files under a built dist directory and pin them via a pinning provider endpoint. That scripted approach is repeatable and fits nicely into a CI step. The core idea is to authenticate to the pinning service using A P I credentials, walk the dist directory, and call the client's add or addAll method with pinning options and the wrapWithDirectory flag. A concrete run: after setting environment variables for the A P I key and secret, you run the deploy script on a CI runner or locally to produce a root CID you can share. A key security note covered in the chapter is never to hardcode A P I credentials in source or frontend bundles. Use environment variables or secrets storage in your CI provider: for GitHub Actions store the Pinata keys in repository secrets and reference them in the workflow file. A common misconception is that treating A P I keys like config is sufficient; in reality they grant write/pinning access and must be rotated if exposed. Finally, inspect the resulting log output for the root CID and store it as a deployment artifact in your CI pipeline so downstream jobs (like ENS updates) can consume it. A final question: where in your CI pipeline will you store the generated CID so subsequent steps can update ENS or notify stakeholders?

keyIdea.title: Automated uploads must protect secrets
keyIdea.text: Use environment variables and CI secrets for Pinata credentials; emit the CID as an artifact for subsequent automation steps like ENS updates.

content.html:
Module 8 › Chapter 8.8 › Deployment Script
deploy-ipfs.js
Essential pattern: authenticate, collect files, call addAll with pin=true.
// Example: collect and upload
const ipfs = create({ host: 'ipfs.pinata.cloud', port: 5001, protocol: 'https', headers: { authorization: auth } });
for await (const file of ipfs.addAll(getFiles(buildPath), { pin: true, wrapWithDirectory: true })) {
  // log file.path and file.cid
}
// The script prints the root CID for use in CI.
API Key Safety
Never commit keys. Use a .env locally and secrets in CI. Rotate keys if exposed and restrict API permissions where possible.
CI Integration Pattern
  1. Checkout code, run tests.
  2. Run npm run build to produce dist.
  3. Run the deploy script using CI secrets to upload and pin the dist folder.
  4. Store the root CID as a pipeline artifact and optionally call a step to update ENS.
Pro Tip

Emit the CID as a simple JSON artifact so later workflow steps can parse and use it without manual copy-paste.

screens.title: Activity: publish and verify your dApp — assessment checklist
screens.subtitle: A practical checklist to deploy manually and validate the result

narration.text: This hands-on activity walks you through publishing your dApp and verifying it, then offers assessment checks you can use to confirm competence. Start by running the production build command in your project and confirm a dist (or build) folder exists with index. html and the compiled assets. Next, use the Pinata web interface to upload the dist folder: add files → folder → select dist. Pinata will return a CID once the upload completes. Open the gateway URL with that CID in a browser and verify the app loads. For the assessment, perform three checks: first, confirm that the site loads from the CID across two different public gateways; second, connect a wallet and perform a read-only call plus a simple transaction if available; third, demonstrate updating an ENS contenthash if you control a domain or describe the steps to do so if you cannot. A common pitfall is leaking A P I keys: show where you stored keys (local. env or CI secrets) and why they are safe. The assessment question in the chapter asks why IPFS hosting is preferred over centralized servers for censorship resistance — your answer should mention immutability, content addressing, and pinning. Complete this activity and keep the CID and deployment notes as evidence. Which test did you find most informative when validating your deployed dApp?

screens.subtitle: Three core ideas to retain from this chapter

narration.text: These compact concept cards collect the essentials: what IPFS is, why decentralized hosting matters, and what a pinning service like Pinata does. IPFS provides content-addressed storage using cryptographic CIDs for immutability and verifiable integrity. Decentralized hosting avoids single points of failure and reduces censorship risk by serving frontend files from a peer-to-peer network. Pinata and other pinning services ensure your CID remains available on the IPFS network by retaining copies on reliable nodes. Keep these three ideas in mind when you deploy: files are identified by content, not location; availability depends on pinning; and ENS is a human-facing pointer that you can update when you publish new CIDs. Which single one of these will change how you publish your next dApp? IPFS

Pinata

Summary
Together these concepts enable a resilient, content-addressed frontend that you can publish, verify, and point at with ENS for a human-friendly experience.

narration.text: Keep three operational reminders in mind: understand CIDs and immutability, secure your pinning credentials and CI secrets, and plan an update workflow that uses ENS or artifacts to point users to the latest version. The CID is your canonical artifact identifier; when it changes, consider how users, bookmarks, and ENS records will be updated. Protect your pinning A P I keys in environment variables or CI secret storage and never expose them to frontend code. Finally, a deployment checklist and verification steps — gateway checks, wallet connectivity, and contract calls — will save time and prevent surprises in production. Module 8 › Chapter 8.8 › Operational Reminders
CID = Artifact
Record and publish the CID for each release; use it to verify exact deployed bundles.
Protect secrets
Keep Pinata keys in CI secrets and .env files locally; never bundle them into the frontend.
Verify runtime
After publishing, test on gateways, connect a wallet, and run sample contract calls to confirm behavior.
One-sentence takeaway
Treat publishing as a release process: build, pin, verify, and update pointers or documentation so users always reach the correct, pinned artifact.
